definition: Software you rent by subscription and use in a browser instead of buying once and installing. You pay for access, and the vendor handles hosting, updates, and security.
why_it_matters: Nearly every product on PlanPrice is SaaS, so the pricing question is never the sticker price — it is the total cost over the years you will use it. Compare subscription totals across two or three years, not month one, and remember that when you stop paying, access ends: your data export plan matters as much as the monthly rate.

definition: A pricing model where you pay per user login, sometimes called per-seat or per-user pricing. Adding a team member raises the bill; removing one lowers it.
why_it_matters: Seat-based pricing punishes growth in headcount, so model the bill at your twelve-month team size, not today's. Watch for seat minimums — Monday.com requires three seats on paid plans — and contrast with unlimited-user models like Xero, where you pay for features instead of logins. Always ask what guests, viewers, and your accountant cost.

definition: Plans stacked in levels — Starter, Pro, Enterprise — where each tier unlocks more features, higher limits, or better support. Most B2B software is sold this way.
why_it_matters: The middle tier is engineered to look like the sensible choice, so ignore the framing and map your must-have features to tiers directly. The expensive mistake is buying the top tier for one feature — check whether that feature is available as an add-on, or whether the tier below plus a workaround covers you.

definition: Pricing tied to how much you use — transactions processed, emails sent, API calls made — rather than a flat fee. The bill scales with your activity.
why_it_matters: Usage-based pricing is gentle when you are small and can surprise you at scale, so model the bill at three volume levels: today, a good month, and a great month. Compare it against flat-rate alternatives by computing the effective rate — total cost divided by total usage — rather than comparing sticker prices.

definition: A free tier that is genuinely useful, with paid upgrades for power features. The vendor bets you will grow into paying.
why_it_matters: Evaluate a free tier by what it omits, not what it includes: HubSpot's free CRM, Wave's free accounting, Square's free POS software, and Calendly's free single event type are all real starting points. Find the exact trigger that forces the first paid invoice — a contact limit, a second event type, a feature gate — and price year two, not month one.

definition: The choice between paying month-to-month or prepaying a year, usually for a discount. Annual billing trades commitment for a lower effective rate.
why_it_matters: Only take the annual discount after a full cycle on monthly billing — you want proof the tool survives your worst month before you prepay. Seasonal businesses should be especially careful, and always check the cancellation terms: some annual plans refund nothing if you leave in month three.

definition: A one-time charge for setup, data migration, or training when you start. Sometimes waived, sometimes mandatory, sometimes disguised as implementation.
why_it_matters: Add the onboarding fee to the year-one total before comparing vendors — a cheaper monthly rate with a steep setup fee often loses. Ask exactly what the fee covers, whether migration help is included, and whether it can be waived; it frequently can be, but only if you ask before signing.

definition: The length of your commitment and what happens when it ends — many B2B contracts auto-renew for another full term unless you cancel inside a notice window.
why_it_matters: Put the cancellation deadline in your calendar the day you sign, because the auto-renewal notice window is easy to miss and expensive to discover. Check whether renewal pricing is locked or can rise, and prefer vendors whose renewal terms are stated up front over ones you have to ask about twice.

definition: A service-level agreement (SLA) is the vendor's contractual promise about uptime and support response times, plus what you receive if they miss. Standard in infrastructure and payments, rarer in small-business tools.
why_it_matters: When comparing tools your business depends on daily, an SLA turns a marketing uptime claim into a contractual one — but read the remedy, which is usually service credits, not cash, and note the exclusions. For most small-business software the practical comparison is simpler: how fast does support actually answer when something breaks.

definition: A time-limited period of full or nearly-full access before you pay. The honest way to evaluate software — if you use it properly.
why_it_matters: A trial only works if you trial with real data and real workflows — sample projects flatter every tool. Check whether the trial requires a credit card up front and what happens when it ends: automatic billing, a hard stop, or a downgrade to a free tier. Set a calendar reminder two days before it expires.

definition: Moving your existing data — customers, transactions, history — into the new tool. The most underestimated cost in any software switch.
why_it_matters: Ask what migration help is included free versus billed extra, and test the import with a slice of real data during the trial — deduplication and custom-field mapping are where migrations stall. Just as important is the reverse: confirm you can export everything in a standard format before you import anything.

definition: An API lets software talk to your other tools programmatically; integrations are pre-built connections. Both determine whether the tool fits the stack you already run.
why_it_matters: Check whether API access requires a higher tier — some vendors gate it above the plans most small businesses buy. Then test the two or three integrations you will actually use rather than admiring the app-directory logo wall; a native-feeling connection to your calendar or inbox beats fifty logos.

definition: Whether the vendor bills and operates in your currency — and what happens when it does not. List-price currency and billing currency are different questions.
why_it_matters: For Canadian buyers this is a first-pass filter: FreshBooks, Wave, and QuickBooks bill in CAD, and Shopify bills Canadian merchants in CAD at checkout, while Xero lists in USD. Beyond the sticker, ask how the product handles CAD bank feeds and tax categories — billing in your currency means little if the bookkeeping does not follow.

definition: A fee charged on each sale or payment processed — typically a small percentage plus a fixed amount. The core of payment-processor pricing.
why_it_matters: Do not compare the headline rate; compare the effective rate — total fees divided by total volume — computed from a real month of your sales. Flat-rate structures like Square's suit smaller or spikier volume, while interchange-plus suits higher steady volume, and the crossover only shows up in your own numbers.

definition: Grandfathering means existing customers keep their old price when rates rise; a price lock is a contractual guarantee the price will not change for a set period.
why_it_matters: Introductory discounts expire, so the price that matters is the renewal price — get it in writing before you sign. Ask whether the vendor has a history of grandfathering existing customers through increases, and treat a first-year quote as a sales tool, not a promise.
